tagline: Marshes, waterways and working landscapes frame the places of Tubman’s life.
intro: The Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad Byway winds through Eastern Shore landscapes and waterways, linking Cambridge with Goldsboro over 125 miles. Maryland’s tourism office allows three to four hours for the drive and recommends two to three days to explore. The Federal Highway Administration presents this All-American Road as a journey through working landscapes commemorating Tubman and the enslaved and free people involved in the Underground Railroad.

The Underground Railroad was a secret network of roads, waterways, trails and hiding places used by people fleeing slavery before the Civil War. Tubman learned navigation and survival skills while working beside her father, Ben Ross, in Madison. After securing her own freedom, she returned to the Poplar Neck area to rescue her brothers and later her parents. The modern byway interprets places where she lived, worked and led others out of slavery.

From Cambridge, the route heads west toward Church Creek, then south to the Tubman visitor center and east through Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge. It passes near Brodess Farm and turns north through Bucktown before returning toward Cambridge. Continue through East New Market to Linchester’s gristmill and the James Webb Cabin near Preston, then toward Denton, Greensboro and Goldsboro. Beyond Maryland, the larger driving tour continues through Delaware to Philadelphia, where Tubman first found freedom.

moments.title: Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge
moments.text: Blackwater’s landscape includes freshwater impoundments, brackish tidal wetlands, open fields and forests of evergreen and deciduous trees. The refuge covers more than 28,000 acres on Maryland’s Eastern Shore, twelve miles south of Cambridge. The refuge was established in 1933 as a sanctuary for waterfowl migrating along the Atlantic Flyway. Its protected birds include bald eagles, while winter brings migrating geese and ducks. Maryland’s tourism office includes the refuge’s water trails and Wildlife Drive in its Tubman itinerary. The byway itself crosses the refuge on Key Wallace Drive before passing near Brodess Farm, where Tubman spent her younger years.

moments.title: Bucktown
moments.text: At Bucktown Village Store, the teenage Harriet Tubman tried to help an enslaved man avoid capture and was nearly killed. Maryland’s tourism office dates this act of defiance to around 1835. Tubman had spent her early years enslaved at the nearby Brodess Farm, the plantation associated with her childhood in the Bucktown community. The byway brings these places together: it passes near the farm, then follows Bucktown Road north to the store. The Bucktown Village Foundation operates the restored general store, preserving a place associated with this early resistance to slavery.

moments.title: James Webb Cabin
moments.text: The 1852 James Webb Cabin near Preston stands on ballast stones from ships. Maryland’s tourism office identifies it as the Eastern Shore’s only surviving pre-Civil War log dwelling known to have been built by and for an African American. The cabin stands along what may have been an Underground Railroad route used by Tubman and her parents.
